source.title: Are running speeds maximized with simple-spring stance mechanics?

paper.citation: Clark, K. P., & Weyand, P. G. (2014). Are running speeds maximized with simple-spring stance mechanics? Journal of Applied Physiology, 117(6), 604–615. https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00174.2014
paper.abstract: Do competitive sprinters attain their fastest speeds with the symmetric force–time pattern predicted by a passive linear spring-mass model? Participants: 14 athletes, comprising seven competitive sprinters and seven athlete nonsprinters. Sport and level: Intercollegiate team-sport athletes through professional/world-class track sprinters. Training context: Repeated treadmill trials at 5.0 m/s, 7.0 m/s, and individual top speed. Boundary: Laboratory treadmill sprinting; the study did not test a training intervention or field-sport performance. Cross-sectional biomechanical comparison of specialization group and running speed. Vertical ground-reaction-force waveforms were collected at 1,000 Hz on a high-speed force treadmill; 797 footfalls entered formal hypothesis tests. Agreement with a half-sine spring-mass prediction was quantified with R² and RMSE; a two-factor group-by-speed ANOVA tested the hypotheses.
paper.tldr: This paper informs interpretation of force–time mechanics during maximal sprinting and the limits of applying a simple spring-mass model to high-speed athletes. Competitive sprinters reached a higher mean top speed than nonsprinters (10.36 ± 0.27 vs 8.72 ± 0.29 m/s) and produced greater mean stance-averaged vertical force (2.20 ± 0.03 vs 1.99 ± 0.04 body weights). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional biomechanical comparison of specialization group and running speed. Vertical ground-reaction-force waveforms were collected at 1,000 Hz on a high-speed force treadmill; 797 footfalls entered formal hypothesis tests. Agreement with a half-sine spring-mass prediction was quantified with R² and RMSE; a two-factor group-by-speed ANOVA tested the hypotheses.
paper.findings: Competitive sprinters reached a higher mean top speed than nonsprinters (10.36 ± 0.27 vs 8.72 ± 0.29 m/s) and produced greater mean stance-averaged vertical force (2.20 ± 0.03 vs 1.99 ± 0.04 body weights). Sprinters' waveform agreement with the simple-spring model was lower at top speed (R² < 0.80; RMSE > 0.55 body weights) than at 5.0–7.0 m/s (R² 0.83–0.85; RMSE 0.43–0.44 body weights), whereas nonsprinters changed little across speeds. The two world-class men showed greater departure from the spring pattern than the two sub-elite men (mean R² 0.71 vs 0.83), an observational performance-gradient result rather than evidence of a trainable causal mechanism.
paper.limitations: The R² = 0.90 cutoff used to label relatively good versus poor spring-model agreement was explicitly described as somewhat subjective. The small, heterogeneous sample and treadmill setting constrain generalization to collegiate American-football sprinting, overground acceleration, and women-specific conclusions. Repeated footfalls are not independent athlete-level replications; the athlete, not the 797 contacts, is the relevant unit for transfer judgments.
paper.practicalImplications: The results support treating simple spring-mass outputs as an incomplete description of maximal sprinting. For collegiate American-football monitoring, force–time waveform shape may add context, but the study does not establish that deliberately increasing asymmetry improves speed or that treadmill thresholds transfer directly to field acceleration.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. The results support treating simple spring-mass outputs as an incomplete description of maximal sprinting. For collegiate American-football monitoring, force–time waveform shape may add context, but the study does not establish that deliberately increasing asymmetry improves speed or that treadmill thresholds transfer directly to field acceleration. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
